# Stop Writing From Scratch: Build an Editorial Desk With Claude Code

> **Verdict**
>
> - A sellable article system starts with reusable evidence, not a longer draft.
> - Claude Code can organize research, drafts, and distribution material in one workspace; it is not useful only to people shipping software.
> - Keep the judgment human: verify sources, label uncertainty, and never turn generated text into a claim you cannot stand behind.

You finish researching an article, then lose an afternoon making the bonus, a social post, and a follow-up idea from scratch. The bottleneck is rarely writing speed. It is the fact that the evidence disappears into the finished post.

This is a practical workflow for Japanese-language solo creators who sell paid posts, newsletters, affiliate content, or their own products. The aim is modest: turn one research topic into a long article, a useful bonus, and a short post without pretending that automation guarantees sales.

## Start with the reader's next move

Write one sentence before opening a research tab: “A solo creator who sells paid content can turn one researched topic into an article and distribution material they can reuse.” Then name the next action: create an evidence note, an article outline, a one-page bonus, and one post.

That constraint matters. Without it, a tool review becomes a list of features. With it, every source has a job: it either helps the reader decide, helps them do the work, or does not belong in this piece.

## Treat the research folder as the first draft

Do not ask an agent for an essay first. Make a small evidence file first. For each source, record the URL, the exact claim it supports, and whether you personally checked the claim. Put unverified ideas in a separate section.

Apify's public writing program is a useful example of why this distinction matters. It says writers receive $500 after an article is reviewed and ready for publication, but it also asks for original, previously unpublished work and practical experience with the topic. The lesson is not “write an article and get paid.” The lesson is that useful content has conditions: real work, evidence, editorial review, and an audience fit.

Use Claude Code after the notes exist. Ask it to separate facts from proposals, group repeated evidence, list the reader's likely questions, and produce a checklist from the sources. It can save the clerical pass. It cannot supply the observation you did not make.

## Split one research topic into four different jobs

The long article, bonus, social post, and next idea should share evidence but not repeat each other.

| Asset | Reader need | What to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long article | A reasoned decision | claim, evidence, limit, process |
| Paid bonus | A starting point | template, checklist, prompt, example |
| Short post | A reason to care now | one concrete scene and one reversal |
| Idea note | A faster next cycle | discarded angles and open questions |

Write them in that order. Start with the evidence, then write the long article. Make the bonus from the steps that readers will actually repeat. Write the post last, once you know the one tension the article resolves. A post written first can force a nuanced article into a slogan.

## What the agent can do, and what stays with you

Let the agent detect duplicate notes, produce section options, turn a confirmed procedure into a checklist, and flag claims without a cited source. Keep these decisions for yourself: whether a source supports the sentence next to it, whether a case study is representative, and where a paid preview should stop.

The public TECHi author page makes a similar distinction in another context. It describes front-page and newsletter distribution plus revenue share, while setting a 1 million combined-follower threshold for its author tier. Distribution is not a universal promise. Conditions decide whether an opportunity applies.

Give the agent boundaries in plain language: do not blend facts and suggestions; retain source URLs; do not claim personal results that are not verified; and state the limits beside the mechanism. Those instructions make later editing easier because you can trace a paragraph back to an actual source.

## A 90-minute first run

Choose one topic, find three primary sources, write one conclusion, make one template, and draft one short post. At the end, add a single line: “Which source changed the reader's next action?” That line becomes the starting point for the next article.

Creators who publish consistently are not inventing a new system each time. They are recovering the research work they already paid for with their attention.

## Try the workflow

If you want one workspace for keeping research, article work, and release steps visible, [see the Life Manager workflow](https://aniccaai.com/lm?product_id=anicca&run_id=20261011-134916&artifact_id=article-en&variant_id=editorial-desk-workflow&click_id=20261011-134916-article-en). Start by saving the evidence note for your next piece.
